reason: The passage features several non-royal, administrative officials who demonstrate clear agency: Eliakim (אֶלְיָקִ֣ים בֶּן־ חִלְקִיָּ֖ה), Shebna the scribe (שֶׁבְנָ֣ה הַסֹּפֵ֔ר), and Joah son of Asaph (יוֹאָ֥ח בֶּן־ אָסָ֖ף). These men take purposeful action throughout the narrative—they approach Rab-shakeh to negotiate language preferences, consult with the king, deliver messages, and participate in strategic decisions. They are not royalty themselves nor divine figures, making them 'regular people' relative to the kings (Hezekiah and Sennacherib) and prophet (Isaiah) who dominate the narrative. Their agency is evident in their ability to act, speak, influence events, and make independent decisions within the political and military crisis, even though they operate within an official hierarchy.
